claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The starting material has a uniform, single-phase fcc matrix.
The starting material has demonstrated high strength and fatigue performance.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by selective elemental segregation at the alloy surface.
Selective surface segregation triggers the formation of distinct oxide scales.
Al, Ti, and Cr preferentially migrate to the surface under thermal activation because of their oxidation potentials and interactions with the other alloying elements.
Under oxidizing conditions, enrichment of Al, with lesser contributions from Ti and Cr, produces a coherent alumina/chromia scale.
The adherent oxide scale limits further oxygen ingress.
Formation of the protective oxide scale minimizes underlying structural degradation and preserves the fcc matrix.
Formation of the protective oxide scale preserves strength, fatigue performance, and mechanical reliability.
Under reducing conditions, insufficient oxygen suppresses formation of a coherent protective scale.
Reducing exposure produces unstable or discontinuous oxide features.
Failure to form a coherent scale in reducing conditions leads to deeper internal oxidation.
Reducing exposure causes void formation and phase destabilization.
Reducing exposure leads to measurable reductions in fatigue strength and overall structural integrity relative to the starting state.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply around 900 degrees Celsius under the specified oxygen-rich and hydrogen-rich gas compositions.
Additive-manufacturing-induced microsegregation or defects may influence oxidation behavior.
